catalog_quote: [Eloranta 2020:126] In relation to stress, the inconsistent use of the accent marks in all sources leads to various tentative interpretations. Stark (1968: 27) considers stress in Mochica unpredictable and therefore phonemic. She nevertheless assumes that it most often occured on the penultimate syllable. Cerrón-Palomino (1995: 133-138), after going over all Mochica material available ... concludes that the stress had a fixed, antepenultimate position. Hovdhaugen (2004:14) tries to interpret the use of accents by Carrera (1644) and determines that the stress fell on the vowel of the initial syllable. Cerrón-Palomino’s antepenult and Stark’s penult depart from assuming that the Mochica word had three syllables. new_statements.rule_in_words: Extinct language known only from written records with inconsistent diacritics; stress placement is reconstructed and disputed. Eloranta (following Hovdhaugen 2004) holds that stress fell on the root syllable, i.e. the initial syllable (roots mostly monosyllabic, suffixes unstressed, the reduced vowel <ae> never accented and prone to syncope). Cerrón-Palomino 1995 (also on file, pp.133-138) argues from Oré, Martínez Compañón, Brüning and Lehmann that the native pattern was 'llana o grave' (penultimate, e.g. loan costal > kóstaj), predictable and non-contrastive, though his closing sentence says 'antepenúltima'; Stark 1968 called it phonemic but mostly penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Eloranta ch.10 (p. ~PDF 400): a handful of words with final accent in Carrera (<lapà> 'calabash container', <munà> 'mummy ancestor', <yanà> 'servant', plus <patà>) are 'not typical in Mochica at all' and taken as Quingnam/Quechua loans. Middendorf 1892:52 and Cerrón-Palomino 1995:135 fn.89: the long genitive ending -ō carries the accent and is pronounced almost as a separate word. Cerrón-Palomino: apparent proparoxytones in Lehmann/Brüning (ónceke, súpite) are due to paragogic/epenthetic vowels in the obsolescent stage; final-stressed toponyms (Etén, Monsefú) are Hispanicized.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, reconstructed philologically from 17th-20th c. transcriptions (Oré 1607, Carrera 1644, Martínez Compañón 1780s, Middendorf 1892, Brüning, Lehmann 1929); no phrase-level description beyond Stark's remark (reported by Cerrón-Palomino p.138) that Middendorf's kumó vs. mo kúmo might show a phrase-level accent. All authors stress that the diacritics in Carrera and Middendorf primarily mark vowel quantity, not intensity.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe colonial/republican Mochica (Yunga of Trujillo-Lambayeque; Carrera 1644 = Reque variety, Middendorf 1892 = Eten variety, the last place it was spoken), glottocode moch1259, ISO omc. The language is extinct (last rememberers early-mid 20th c.); every stress claim is a philological reconstruction from inconsistent diacritics, not an observation of speech. Note the PUCP repository titles Cerrón-Palomino's book 'La lengua de Nailamp' but the printed title is 'La lengua de Naimlap'.

VI 'Régimen acentual', pp.133-138 (PDF pp.137-142): neither Carrera 1644 nor Middendorf 1892 says anything about intensity accent; Carrera's and Middendorf's diacritics mark vowel quantity, not stress. Oré 1607 and Martínez Compañón's list suggest penultimate stress; Brüning and Lehmann's accented transcriptions give the basic pattern as 'llana o grave' (penultimate), with apparent proparoxytones explained as paragogic/epenthetic vowels of the obsolescent stage; Brüning's hispanism <kóstaj> < costal 'ilustra perfectamente la colocación automática del acento en la penúltima sílaba'. Only remark: genitive ending -ō 'ist lang und trägt nicht nur den Accent, sondern wird sogar etwas getrennt ausgesprochen' (par. 14-15, p.52). Confirms Cerrón-Palomino's report that Middendorf is silent on stress placement.
